title: DepEd Science MATATAG Curriculum — Grade 3 Life Science

customLessons.title: Scientific Inquiry in Life Science
objectives: Formulate questions and make scientific observations of living organisms using the five senses and hand lenses.
Record qualitative and quantitative observations of plants and small animals in an inquiry journal.
Differentiate living organisms from non-living objects through guided classroom investigations.
customLessons.content:
Life Science is the systematic study of living things, including plants, animals, and microorganisms. Biologists use scientific inquiry to understand how living organisms survive, grow, and interact with the world around them.

Scientific inquiry begins with curious questions and careful observations. Using scientific tools like magnifying hand lenses, measuring rulers, and inquiry journals, young scientists observe details like leaf vein patterns, insect legs, and root structures without harming the specimens.

Observations are classified as qualitative (descriptions using words like green, fuzzy, or fragrant) and quantitative (measurements using numbers like 5 leaves or 12 centimeters tall).

slides.title: Scientific Inquiry in Life Science
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 1 Life Science

Become a young biologist: Discover how scientists observe, question, and investigate the living world.

slides.title: Tools of the Young Biologist
slides.content:
Essential tools for studying living organisms:
• Hand Lens / Magnifying Glass: Enlarge leaf veins, insect antennae, and soil microbes
• Metric Ruler & Tape: Measure plant height and leaf width accurately
• Science Inquiry Journal: Sketch specimens and log daily growth
• Ethical Care: Always observe living creatures gently and return them safely to nature!

slides.title: Qualitative vs Quantitative Observations
slides.content:
Two Ways to Record Science Data:
• Qualitative: Describing observable qualities using senses
  - 'The caterpillar is bright green, smooth, and moves slowly'
• Quantitative: Describing measurable quantities with numbers
  - 'The caterpillar is 4 cm long and weighs 2 grams'
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Choose a plant leaf or small insect
Step 2: Note color, texture, and smell (Qualitative)
Step 3: Measure length in millimeters with a ruler (Quantitative)
Step 4: Record findings neatly in your science notebook

slides.title: Field Study: Philippine Wildlife
slides.content:
How Filipino naturalists study nature:
• Observing Philippine sunbirds pollinating banana blossoms
• Counting egg clusters of tree frogs during monsoon rains
• Identifying native flowering orchids in national parks

slides.title: Classroom Inquiry Check
slides.content:
A pupil writes: 'The garden sunflower has 18 bright yellow petals.' Which part is a quantitative observation?
A) 'Bright yellow'
B) 'Garden sunflower'
C) '18 petals'
D) 'Smells sweet'

Correct Answer: C ('18 petals' uses a countable number!)

customLessons.title: Characteristics and Life Processes of Living Things
objectives: Identify the fundamental characteristics of living things (growth, movement, nutrition, respiration, excretion, response to stimuli, reproduction).
Compare life processes in plants and animals.
Explain how living organisms respond to changes in their immediate environment.
customLessons.content:
All living things share fundamental characteristics that set them apart from non-living matter: they grow, move, consume nutrients, breathe, excrete waste, respond to stimuli, and reproduce.

Plants make their own food through sunlight and show tropisms (growing toward light or gravity). Animals actively move from place to place using legs, wings, or fins to find food and shelter.

Living things respond to external stimuli: a mimosa plant (Makahiya) folds its leaves when touched; animals seek shade when it gets too hot; earthworms burrow into moist soil when exposed to bright sunlight.

slides.title: Characteristics of Living Things
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 1 Life Science

Learn the 7 life processes that define living organisms on planet Earth.

slides.title: The 7 Signs of Life
slides.content:
Every living organism performs these processes:
1. Movement: Active locomotion or slow plant bending
2. Respiration: Exchanging gases to release energy
3. Sensitivity: Responding to environmental stimuli
4. Growth: Increasing in size and developing complexity
5. Reproduction: Producing offspring to continue the species
6. Excretion: Eliminating cellular waste products
7. Nutrition: Absorbing or making food nutrients

slides.title: Plants vs Animals in Action
slides.content:
Comparing Life Processes:
• Feeding: Plants synthesize food via photosynthesis; animals ingest food
• Movement: Animals walk, fly, or swim; plants turn leaves toward the Sun (phototropism)
• Breathing: Animals inhale oxygen through lungs/gills; plants exchange gases via leaf stomata
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Place a potted bean plant near a window
Step 2: Observe stem bending toward sunlight
Step 3: Touch a Makahiya leaf and watch it fold
Step 4: Conclude: Plants actively respond to stimuli!

slides.title: Sensitivity: Responding to Stimuli
slides.content:
How living things react to keep safe:
• Makahiya plant folds its leaves when touched to deter herbivores
• Dogs pant and drink water when overheated
• Earthworms burrow deeper into soil when sunlight hits their skin

slides.title: Living vs Non-Living Quiz
slides.content:
A toy robot can walk, speak words, and uses battery power. Why is it still considered non-living?
A) It is too small
B) It cannot grow, reproduce, or possess living cells
C) It has bright plastic colors
D) It moves on wheels

Correct Answer: B (Non-living objects do not grow, heal, or reproduce!)

customLessons.title: Basic Needs of Living Things
objectives: Identify the basic survival needs of plants and animals: water, food/nutrients, air, sunlight, and shelter/space.
Describe what happens when living organisms are deprived of one or more basic needs.
Relate basic needs to the welfare and care of household pets, farm animals, and crops.
customLessons.content:
All living organisms require essential resources from their environment to survive and thrive.

Plants require sunlight, water, carbon dioxide from the air, soil nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium), and space to spread their roots and leaves.

Animals require clean water, nutritious food, oxygen to breathe, and safe shelter to protect themselves from predators and harsh weather.

Depriving an organism of its basic needs leads to stunted growth, wilting, disease, or death. Caring for pets, farm animals, and trees requires providing these necessities consistently.

slides.title: Basic Needs of Living Things
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 2 Life Science

Explore the essential resources that keep all plants, animals, and humans alive.

slides.title: What Green Plants Need
slides.content:
Five essentials for plant life:
1. Sunlight: Energy source for food production
2. Water: Carries minerals and maintains turgor pressure
3. Carbon Dioxide: Carbon building block for glucose
4. Soil Nutrients: Essential minerals (N-P-K) for cell growth
5. Space: Adequate room for roots and spreading branches

slides.title: What Animals Need to Survive
slides.content:
Four essentials for animal life:
1. Nutritious Food: Energy for muscles, growth, and body warmth
2. Clean Water: Solvent for blood, cooling, and digestion
3. Oxygen Gas: Required for cellular respiration
4. Safe Shelter & Space: Protection from heavy rains, heat, and predators
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Check your pet's water bowl daily
Step 2: Provide nutritious age-appropriate food
Step 3: Ensure dry, ventilated sleeping shelter
Step 4: Allow exercise space for healthy development

slides.title: Deprivation: What Happens When Needs Are Missing?
slides.content:
Effects of lacking basic needs:
• No water: Plant leaves wilt, lose cell pressure, and dry out
• No sunlight: Plant leaves turn pale yellow and cannot produce food
• No food: Animals lose weight, become weak, and succumb to illness

slides.title: Basic Needs Check Quiz
slides.content:
What vital gas in the air do dogs, birds, fish, and humans breathe in to stay alive?
A) Carbon dioxide
B) Oxygen
C) Helium
D) Nitrogen only

Correct Answer: B (Oxygen gas is required by animals for respiration!)

customLessons.title: Structure and Function of Organisms
objectives: Identify the external body parts of common animals and explain their functions.
Identify the major vegetative and reproductive organs of flowering plants and their functions.
Relate specialized anatomical structures to specific survival tasks.
customLessons.content:
Living things have specialized body parts called structures, and each structure performs a specific job called a function.

In plants: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water from soil; stems support branches and transport sap; leaves capture sunlight for photosynthesis; flowers enable reproduction; fruits protect seeds.

In animals: Eyes, ears, and noses detect predators and food; legs, wings, and fins enable locomotion; claws, beaks, and teeth gather and process food; fur and scales provide protection.

Specialized structures match survival needs: ducks have webbed feet for paddling; eagles have hooked talons for catching fish; cacti have needle-like spines to reduce water loss.

slides.title: Structure and Function of Organisms
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 2 Life Science

Discover how specialized body parts help plants and animals survive and succeed.

slides.title: Plant Structures & Their Functions
slides.content:
The 5 Major Organs of Plants:
• Roots: Anchor plant into soil; absorb water and dissolved minerals
• Stem: Supports aerial branches and transports fluids between roots and leaves
• Leaves: The solar food factories performing photosynthesis
• Flowers: Colorful structures attracting pollinators for reproduction
• Fruits & Seeds: Protect developing seeds and aid dispersal

slides.title: Animal Structures: Movement & Feeding
slides.content:
Matching form to function:
• Fins & Streamlined Body (Fish): Slicing through water with minimal drag
• Webbed Feet (Ducks): Paddle-like surface for swimming
• Sharp Curved Talons (Eagles): Grasping and holding slippery fish
• Grinding Molars (Carabao): Crushing tough grass fibers
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Look at the feet of a bird
Step 2: Are they webbed, clawed, or grasping?
Step 3: Webbed = Swimming; Talons = Hunting; Claws = Perching
Step 4: Structure always reveals function!

slides.title: Protective Structures
slides.content:
Defensive body armor in nature:
• Turtles: Hard bony carapace shields soft internal organs
• Cacti: Needle-sharp spines deter thirsty desert herbivores
• Porcupines: Modified sharp quills detach to injure attacking predators

slides.title: Organ Function Quiz
slides.content:
Which plant structure is primarily responsible for absorbing water and dissolved minerals from the soil?
A) Flowers
B) Leaves
C) Roots
D) Bark

Correct Answer: C (Roots anchor and absorb water/nutrients!)

customLessons.title: Interactions Among Living Things and Their Environment
objectives: Identify cooperative relationships where living things help one another (mutualism).
Explain the oxygen and carbon dioxide gas exchange between plants and animals.
Describe how living things interact with non-living environmental elements.
customLessons.content:
No organism lives in isolation. Living things constantly interact with other living things (biotic factors) and non-living surroundings (abiotic factors).

Plants and animals depend on each other: plants release oxygen that animals breathe, while animals exhale carbon dioxide that plants use to make food.

Pollination is a key interaction: bees, butterflies, and sunbirds drink flower nectar and simultaneously carry pollen between blossoms, allowing plants to form fruits and seeds.

Animals use non-living materials for habitat: birds build nests with twigs on tree branches; earthworms aerate soil; fish swim in river water.

slides.title: Interactions in the Environment
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 2 Life Science

Discover the web of life: How plants, animals, and non-living elements depend on each other.

slides.title: The Oxygen-Carbon Dioxide Partnership
slides.content:
Nature's Perfect Balance:
• Plants take in Carbon Dioxide (CO2) exhaled by animals and release fresh Oxygen (O2)
• Animals inhale Oxygen (O2) and exhale Carbon Dioxide (CO2)
• Together, plants and animals maintain clean, breathable air on Earth!

slides.title: Pollination: A Win-Win Friendship
slides.content:
Mutual cooperation in nature:
• Flowers provide sweet nectar as food for bees, butterflies, and sunbirds
• Pollinators dust pollen grains across their bodies and carry it to neighboring flowers
• Result: The plant successfully produces delicious fruits and fertile seeds!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Bee visits flower for nectar
Step 2: Sticky pollen coats bee's legs
Step 3: Bee flies to next flower
Step 4: Pollination enables seed and fruit development

slides.title: Living Things Using Non-Living Resources
slides.content:
Biotic organisms utilizing abiotic nature:
• Birds collect mud, grass, and twigs to construct sturdy nests
• Earthworms burrow through soil, creating aeration tunnels that help roots breathe
• Mudfish burrow into moist lakebed mud to survive summer dry spells

slides.title: Ecosystem Interaction Quiz
slides.content:
What gas do plants release during the day that humans and animals need to inhale?
A) Smoke
B) Carbon dioxide
C) Oxygen
D) Helium

Correct Answer: C (Plants produce life-giving oxygen during photosynthesis!)

customLessons.title: Environmental Stewardship and Conservation
objectives: Explain the importance of protecting Philippine plant and animal habitats (forests, rivers, mangroves).
Identify harmful human activities that endanger local ecosystems.
Practice concrete conservation actions: waste segregation, tree planting, and wildlife protection.
customLessons.content:
Environmental stewardship means taking responsibility to care for, protect, and preserve the natural world for present and future generations.

Philippine ecosystems (coral reefs, tropical rainforests, mangrove swamps) are home to unique biodiversity like the Philippine Eagle, Tarsier, and Tamaraw.

Destructive human actions—cutting down forests (deforestation), dumping trash in rivers, and blasting reefs—destroy homes of living things and lead to species endangerment.

Every student can be an environmental steward: planting native trees, conserving water, avoiding plastic waste, participating in river cleanups, and respecting wild animals.

slides.title: Environmental Stewardship & Conservation
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 2 Life Science

Protecting Philippine biodiversity: Caring for our forests, rivers, mangroves, and wildlife.

slides.title: Philippine Biodiversity Treasures
slides.content:
Unique organisms found only in the Philippines (Endemic):
• Philippine Eagle: Magnificent apex predator of Sierra Madre rainforests
• Philippine Tarsier: Tiny nocturnal primate of Bohol
• Tamaraw: Rare dwarf wild buffalo of Mindoro
• Dugong (Sea Cow): Gentle marine herbivore of Palawan seagrass beds

slides.title: Threats to Wildlife Habitats
slides.content:
Human impacts threatening nature:
• Deforestation: Cutting trees leaves birds and primates homeless
• River & Ocean Plastic Pollution: Sea turtles ingest plastic bags mistaking them for jellyfish
• Siltation: Soil runoff smothers living coral reefs
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Sort waste into 4 bins at school
Step 2: Plant native tree seedlings in the garden
Step 3: Turn off taps to save freshwater
Step 4: Spread the word to family and neighbors!

slides.title: Why Mangrove Forests Are Superheroes
slides.content:
Coastal guardians of our islands:
• Roots act as safe nursery schools for baby fish, crabs, and shrimp
• Dense thickets break typhoon waves and protect coastal communities from storm surges
• Traps sediment to prevent ocean muddying

slides.title: Stewardship Challenge Quiz
slides.content:
Which action represents responsible environmental stewardship?
A) Burning plastic garbage in the backyard
B) Planting native mangrove and tree seedlings along riverbanks
C) Keeping wild endangered tarsiers as indoor pets
D) Dumping detergent soap directly into rivers

Correct Answer: B (Tree planting restores habitats and stabilizes soil!)
